entity: Redwood Fabrication, Inc. — C corporation (assumption; prior returns show a federal NOL carryforward, consistent with corporate filing)
event: Discharge of indebtedness on the plan effective date — 9/30/2026 — in a chapter 11 case (Case No. 26-11842-TBM). Plan confirmed 9/2/2026 (Dkt. 214, documents/session3/confirmation_order_excerpt.md); terms as in the term sheet. The GUC balance is discharged on the effective date, 9/30/2026.
debt_discharged_computation: Allowed general unsecured claims $8,400,000.00 (plan term sheet; restated in Dkt. 214) minus plan payments $8,400,000.00 x 35% = $2,940,000.00 (paid over 24 months, first installment on the effective date — Dkt. 214), leaving $8,400,000.00 - $2,940,000.00 = $5,460,000.00 discharged on the effective date 9/30/2026. DIP facility is NOT discharged — repaid in full from exit financing (term sheet), so it generates no COD income. Pre-petition wage claims within the §507(a)(4) cap and the Apex claim were paid during the case (Dkt. 9; Dkt. 48) — also no discharge there.
exclusion_authority: 26 U.S.C. §108(a)(1)(A) (library: irc_108.md) — discharge occurs in a title 11 case, so the entire $5,460,000.00 is excluded from gross income. The threshold question whether the discharge 'occurs in a title 11 case' is answered on these facts: the plan was confirmed 9/2/2026 and the balance was discharged on the effective date 9/30/2026, both inside the chapter 11 case (Dkt. 214).
year_of_discharge: 2026 either way. Both candidate dates — confirmation (9/2/2026) and the effective date (9/30/2026) — fall in the same taxable year (calendar 2026 assumed; the file never states the tax year — flag), so the 'year of discharge' for §108(b) purposes is 2026 regardless of which timing convention applies. WHEN a title 11 discharge occurs (confirmation vs. effective date) is a rule NOT in the library — labeled unverified; immaterial here because both dates are in 2026. The §108(b)(1) reductions are made after the tax for the year of discharge is determined (irc_108.md).

attribute_reduction.other: None. The excluded amount ($5,460,000.00) is applied first to attribute (A), NOLs, per §108(b)(1) (library: irc_108.md): NOL of $6,100,000.00 at petition (term sheet) minus $5,460,000.00 = $640,000.00 remaining. Arithmetic check: 6,100,000 - 5,460,000 = 640,000 (NOT 650,000). Because the NOL fully absorbs the reduction, attributes (B)-(G) — general business credits, minimum tax credit, capital losses, basis of property ($3.2M in fixed assets per term sheet), passive losses, FTCs — are untouched. Caveat: the $6,100,000 figure is the PETITION-date NOL per prior returns; §108(b)(1)(A) reduces the NOL 'for the year of discharge and carryovers.' The year of discharge is 2026 (both 9/2 and 9/30/2026 fall in it), so the reduction base includes the 2026 return year itself — the post-petition stub plus the rest of 2026 — and any 2026 NOL ADDS to the base above $6,100,000, leaving more NOL after the reduction. A short-year split (3/10/2026 petition; short-year rules not in the library — unverified) could change WHICH period is the 'year of discharge' but not the calendar year. The 2026 return/estimated stub NOL is not in the file (QUESTIONS.md) — the $640,000 above is therefore a floor computed on the petition-date figure only; not forced.

election_108b5: No. Under §108(b)(5) (library: irc_108.md) the taxpayer may elect to apply any portion of the reduction first to basis of depreciable property. Do not elect: (1) the NOL carryforward of $6,100,000.00 already absorbs the entire $5,460,000.00 reduction with $640,000.00 to spare, so the default order costs nothing beyond the attribute reduction itself; (2) depreciable-asset basis is only $3,200,000.00 (term sheet) — an election could not even absorb the full reduction and the remaining $5,460,000.00 - $3,200,000.00 = $2,260,000.00 would spill to other attributes anyway; (3) fresh-start reporting is NOT adopted here (see fresh_start.md — test (b) fails), so the entity keeps its historical asset basis for tax purposes and there is no accounting-basis reset that would make sacrificing tax basis a freebie. Net: preserving NOLs and keeping fixed-asset basis intact is the better position on the facts in the file. (Comparative value of an NOL dollar vs. a basis dollar depends on rates and timing not in the file — labeled unverified; conclusion rests on the arithmetic above, which is sufficient.)
